#4208. Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision

A newly identified genetic eye disease can gradually interfere with night vision and the ability to see objects at the edges of the visual field. The condition may be especially difficult to recognize because people can maintain good eyesight for much of their lives before noticeable problems develop.

An international research team, including scientists at the Scheie Eye Institute within the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, traced the condition to a gene already associated with another form of vision loss. However, the two diseases affect eyesight in strikingly different ways. The previously known disorder primarily damages central vision, while the newly discovered condition affects peripheral vision and the ability to see in darkness.

Although the condition has not yet received an official name, researchers are calling it EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration (L-ORD). It is linked to a specific genetic variant known as p.Arg140Trp in the EFEMP1 gene. This change causes an unusually thick accumulation of material between cells in the eye.

A Genetic Discovery That Began Decades Ago

The investigation traces back to 1998, when doctors documented an unusual pattern of vision loss in a family in the United States. As researchers uncovered new genetic evidence, they were able to connect those findings to families in Europe who showed similar symptoms.

The study, published in JAMA Ophthalmology, examined three unrelated families from different countries who carried the p.Arg140Trp variant. Their symptoms were compared with those of another family carrying a different change in the same gene, called p.Arg345Trp, which is associated with the previously recognized disease affecting central vision.

The international collaboration included researchers from Penn Medicine, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Basel, Charles University, and the University of Bonn.

At first, scientists suspected that the unusual symptoms in the original family might be caused by a different genetic disorder. Testing, however, failed to identify the variants responsible for that condition.

"The different disease expression in this family was thought to be similar to a condition caused by C1QTNF5 gene variants. However, none of the variants associated with that disease were found," said Artur V. Cideciyan, PhD, an ophthalmology researcher and co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Our collaborators then discovered a new variant in the EFEMP1 gene that normally causes a different disease where the macula, which is tied to central vision, is affected first."

How the New Eye Disease Affects Night Vision

The researchers found that the newly identified condition develops gradually in the outer regions of the retina. Located at the back of the eye, the retina detects incoming light and transforms it into signals that the brain uses to create visual images.

Unlike the previously known EFEMP1 disorder, which initially affects the macula and central vision, this newly identified disease begins in the peripheral retina. People may see normally for much of their lives before gradually noticing that their side vision is narrowing or that seeing in dim surroundings has become more difficult.

Problems may be particularly noticeable around dusk or at night, when the eyes must rely more heavily on specialized light-sensitive cells called rods.

One reason the disease is challenging to diagnose is that these cells may initially show no visible structural damage. The gradual progression of symptoms can make the condition even harder to recognize.

However, the researchers identified a potentially valuable early clue. In affected individuals, rod cells take unusually long to recover when the eyes move from bright surroundings into darkness. This abnormal response can be detected even when the retina still appears structurally normal.

"We can detect a major abnormality in the way rod photoreceptors recover in darkness with retinas that still look structurally intact," Cideciyan said. "This gives us a functional marker of disease at a stage when photoreceptor cells have not yet been lost."

The finding suggests that changes in how the retina functions may reveal the disease before the light-sensitive cells responsible for vision begin to disappear.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Age-Related Vision Loss

An important question remains unanswered: How many people carry this newly identified genetic variant?

Researchers suspect the condition is relatively uncommon, but they do not yet have enough information to determine its prevalence. Larger investigations will be necessary to establish how frequently the variant occurs and how many people may be affected.

Beyond identifying another inherited eye disorder, the findings could help scientists better understand why vision deteriorates with age. Studying rare genetic diseases can reveal biological processes that may also contribute to much more widespread retinal conditions.

"Aging is a risk factor for many medical conditions, including retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, the most common retinal condition of aging," said Tomas S. Aleman, MD, a professor of ophthalmology and the other co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Lessons learned from these infrequent, late-onset genetic eye diseases offer glimpses at possible mechanisms of disease for much more frequent retinal problems."

By revealing how different changes in a single gene can produce distinct patterns of vision loss, the research adds to scientists' understanding of inherited retinal disease. It also highlights the potential importance of detecting changes in visual function before damage becomes apparent in the retina's structure.

The study received support from the University of Edinburgh Chancellor's Fellowship award, RS Macdonald Charitable Trust Seedcorn Award, the BrightFocus Foundation (M2024009N), the German Research Foundation (532367710), the Medical Research Council (MC_UU_00035/9, MC_UU_00007/10), the Swiss National Science Foundation (204285), the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic (NW24-06-00083), Charles University in Prague (UNCE/24/MED/022 and SVV 2600631), and the Samuel G. Jacobson, MD, PhD, Memorial Fund.

#4205. Toyota is giving the Corolla a radical makeover, including its first 100% electric version

Toyota is overhauling its best-selling vehicle of all time, which will include the first fully electric Corolla.

The Toyota Corolla is one of the most recognized and best-selling automotive nameplates of all time.

Since its debut in 1966, over 57 million drivers have chosen the Corolla thanks to its reliability, low cost of ownership, efficiency, and affordable price tag.

Toyota sells the Corolla in more than 150 countries and has expanded the lineup over the past 50 years from sedans and hatchbacks to coupes, wagons, a sporty GR Corolla, and the Corolla Cross compact SUV.

For its 13th generation, Toyota is planning a major overhaul that’s expected to be its biggest transformation yet.

The next-gen Toyota Corolla will be based on a new “multipathway” platform that will support gas, hybrid, plug-in hybrid, and, for the first time, fully electric powertrains.

“Whether it’s a battery EV, plug-in hybrid, hybrid, or internal combustion engine vehicle ― whatever the power source ― let’s make good-looking cars that everyone will want to drive!” Toyota’s former president and current CEO Koji Sato said after unveiling the Corolla Concept at the Japan Mobility Show last October.

Toyota has kept most details a secret, including battery and powertrain specs. However, the new version is expected to adopt a similar design to the concept.

“When we created the concept, we wanted to give the Corolla name a new twist,” Norihiko Kobayashi, who has led the Corolla program since 2011, told Motor.es during a recent interview.

The Corolla has undergone several minor updates over the past 60 years, but the next-gen model will look nothing like its predecessors.

“It wasn’t simply about following in the footsteps of the past,” Kobayashi explained, “we wanted to delve into the future while still maintaining the Corolla identity.”

Developing the next-gen Corolla “wasn’t just about making a new car, but about redefining the future without looking back,” he added.

Like the current version, the new Toyota Corolla will come in several different body types, including a sedan, hatchback, crossover, and a GR variant.

Details have yet to be confirmed, but the Toyota Corolla EV is expected to be available in single- and dual-motor configurations and offer a pure electric driving range of at least 250 miles.

The hybrid will reportedly use a new 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine and an electric motor. Toyota’s engineers told Car and Driver the hybrid system would deliver around 134 horsepower. It’s also estimated to be 10% to 20% more efficient than the current Corolla.

Toyota’s next-gen Corolla is expected to debut sometime in 2027 as a 2028 model year. According to Car and Driver, the gas version will likely start at around $25,000, the hybrid around $27,000, and the EV and PHEVs will likely be priced in the $30,000 range.

#4204. Battlefield Labs is coming back for a short session to test out next week's Battlefield 6 update, and you can expect more tests in the future, too

Battlefield Labs is evolving, as it reopens its doors for its next - unusual - session.

Battlefield Studios is seemingly trying something different with Battlefield 6’s next patch, which everyone assumed would be a standard, mid-season update not intended to change the game significantly.

However, it appears that it may bring more to the game than we realised, enough that the developer sees it as an excuse to bring back the pre-launch Battlefield Labs testing initiative.

The December 9 patch kicks off the final phase of the game’s first season, which is set to take the game through the holidays and into the new year. We’ve known about its content for a while, and it’s definitely the lightest, compared to the two previous phases.

Battlefield Studios announced a host of new changes that will be included in the same patch, which are apparently significant enough to require player testing. The developer is reviving Battlefield Labs to help it do so, but only for three two-hour sessions, split across the game’s three main server regions (EU, NA, APAC).

All tests are scheduled for today, December 2, and they remain under NDA. Battlefield Labs is also sticking with PC as its chosen platform yet again, though you will be able to join through Steam this time, alongside the EA app.

The focus of the test will be on three key areas that the December 9 patch will be touching. First, there’s footstep audio, an issue that was really brought into focus with the launch of Redsec Battle Royale. You can expect to hear enemy footsteps from farther away, and intuitively know the type of surface they’re moving on.

The patch also brings another pass to hit registration and netcode, which BF Studios says should improve responsiveness in close-quarter situations. Finally, there are broader changes to other combat areas that the announcement didn’t elaborate on.

All testing will take place on Eastwood, and Operation Firestorm, rotating between Conquest, and Escalation.

Going forward, Battlefield Studios said to expect Labs to be open to more players, and for the process itself to be smoother. The developer wants to have faster turnaround times, after all, so that the initiative can test smaller changes and be more responsive to player feedback.

Some of the more involved, future sessions will include experiments with map layout changes and various other non-standard compositions of player and vehicle numbers. Of course, you can also expect new maps and modes to be tested in Labs, similar to how the CTE was used in Battlefield 4’s long life.

#4203. A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat

A widely used blood pressure medication may have an unexpected benefit beyond its ability to control hypertension. Scientists have found that losartan can activate brown fat, a specialized type of body fat that burns energy, and improve metabolic activity in mice. The discovery suggests that an existing medication could potentially be repurposed to stimulate brown fat and support metabolic health.

Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), which have an established safety profile. In a new study published in Nature, researchers found that the drug increased brown fat activity through a biological mechanism separate from its blood pressure effects. This raises the possibility of developing treatments that activate brown fat without lowering blood pressure.

The findings also revealed a surprising connection between brown fat and mental health. After examining data from more than 100,000 patients, researchers discovered that people with detectable brown fat had lower rates of several medical conditions, including anxiety and depression. This is the first time the research team has reported associations between brown fat and psychiatric health, adding to earlier evidence linking the tissue to better cardiovascular and metabolic health.

The research was led by Paul Cohen at Rockefeller University's Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism, working with Heiko Schöder and Daniel Lafontaine from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC). It expands on research published in 2021, when Cohen's team analyzed approximately 50,000 patients and found that those with more brown fat had substantially lower odds of developing cardiometabolic conditions such as coronary artery disease and type II diabetes.

"We only looked for a few diagnostic codes in that study, mainly focusing on cardiovascular disease since that's what this tissue has historically been associated with," says Cohen. "The scope of this new analysis is far more expansive. We doubled our number of patients and considered more than 500 codes, which allowed us to unearth many new insights."

AI Analysis Reveals New Benefits of Brown Fat

To investigate brown fat's relationship with human health, the researchers examined PET/CT scans from more than 100,000 patients who had undergone imaging as part of their cancer monitoring. They focused on scans showing brown adipose tissue, which can be found in six regions of the body, including the neck, armpits, and areas around organs such as the heart and kidneys.

The team used an approach known as reverse translation, which begins with observations in patients and then investigates the biological processes responsible for them. Cohen's laboratory has previously used this strategy to uncover important details about brown fat and its effects on health.

Nicolás Gómez-Banoy, the study's first author and an endocrinologist and instructor in clinical investigation in Cohen's laboratory, used a machine learning system developed by researchers at MSKCC to measure brown fat activity. The technology allowed him to assess both the total activity in each patient and the activity within each of the six anatomical regions.

The analysis showed that brown fat's location could be just as important as its presence. Activity in particular regions appeared to have stronger associations with certain health conditions, suggesting that brown fat may influence the body differently depending on where it is found.

"For example, the axillary, or armpit, area was linked to a decreased risk of high blood pressure compared to other regions," he says. "But overall, patients with brown fat have better glycemic parameters, lipid profiles, and echocardiographic indices, as well as lower inflammatory markers."

These findings indicate that people with brown fat tend to have healthier blood sugar levels, blood fat profiles, measures of heart function, and indicators of inflammation.

Common Blood Pressure Drug Activates Brown Fat

As the researchers investigated medications associated with brown fat activity, they noticed an intriguing pattern. Patients taking angiotensin receptor blockers were more likely to have detectable brown fat on their scans, suggesting that these widely prescribed medications might influence the tissue.

To explore that possibility, the team conducted laboratory experiments using cultured brown fat cells. They found that losartan directly increased the cells' metabolic activity, providing evidence that the drug could stimulate brown fat rather than simply being associated with its presence.

Even more interestingly, the researchers discovered that losartan activated brown fat through molecular pathways different from those responsible for lowering blood pressure. That distinction could be especially valuable for developing future medications that target metabolism without interfering with normal blood pressure regulation.

"The fact that its different effects are mediated by different molecular pathways is advantageous, since it means we could potentially isolate them in future therapies," says Gómez-Banoy. "That way you would be able to stimulate brown fat in people with normal blood pressure."

Additional experiments in healthy mice strengthened the findings. Animals given losartan showed increased energy expenditure, consumed more oxygen, and produced more carbon dioxide, all signs of heightened metabolic activity. Despite these changes, their body weight remained stable.

Brown Fat's Surprising Connection to Mental Health

Beyond its metabolic effects, brown fat may have a previously unrecognized relationship with psychological well-being. The patient analysis revealed that individuals with detectable brown fat had lower rates of anxiety and depression, extending the tissue's potential health associations beyond the cardiovascular system.

"We know that metabolically healthy people tend to have lower incidence of psychiatric diseases, so it could be that having brown fat makes you more metabolically healthy, and this correlates with fewer psychiatric issues," says Gómez-Banoy.

The researchers also found an intriguing relationship involving selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, medications commonly prescribed to treat depression. These drugs appeared to suppress brown fat activity, suggesting another possible connection between psychiatric treatments and metabolic regulation.

However, the findings do not suggest that brown fat is beneficial in every respect. The analysis also identified higher rates of osteoporosis and certain skin diseases among people with brown fat, raising questions about possible trade-offs that require further investigation.

The discoveries have opened several avenues for future research. Scientists hope to examine the genetics of people with particularly high brown fat activity, investigate why the tissue is associated with lower rates of anxiety and depression, and determine whether its apparent benefits can be harnessed safely.

Losartan may also be only one of several existing medications worth investigating. The extensive patient analysis identified additional drugs associated with brown fat activity, offering researchers a range of potential candidates for future studies.

"There were plenty of other medications associated with brown fat activity in our large cohort," Cohen notes. "This is just a start."

Materials provided by Rockefeller University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4201. BYD Ti7 banned from the EU for copying the Land Rover Defender’s design

A Dutch court has barred BYD from selling or building its Ti7 SUV anywhere in the European Union after ruling that it infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s registered design for the Land Rover Defender. Breaking the injunction costs BYD €100,000 per day, up to €10 million.

It’s a sharp turnaround from 10 days ago, when the same court in The Hague handed BYD an early win in the Defender copycat fight. BYD’s Hong Kong shares fell as much as 4% on Monday before closing 1.9% lower.

The preliminary relief judge at the District Court of The Hague issued the ruling on Friday, November 20, in summary proceedings JLR brought against 11 BYD companies.

JLR put six registered EU designs in front of the court. The judge only needed one of them: design 005248580-0004, registered in April 2018 and covering the current Defender 110, known internally as the L663.

According to the ruling, the elements that dominate that design are the rounded “shoulders,” the rounded corners, the signature panel on the C-pillar, the rounded wheel-arch cutouts, the continuous window line, and the overall silhouette. The court found every one of them on the Ti7.

Here’s how the two SUVs compare from the same angles, using official press images from BYD and JLR:

BYD argued that the headlights, grille, bumpers, hood and side profile are all different. Not enough, said the judge, who ruled that those differences, on their own or combined, don’t give an informed user a different overall impression. The court also found the Ti7 sits closer to the Defender than to older boxy SUVs like the Ford Flex, Jeep Wrangler and Mercedes G-Class.

BYD doesn’t sell the Ti7 in the EU. It told the court it has “no concrete plans” to launch it there and that the SUV can only be ordered in the UK.

The judge didn’t buy that as a defense. By BYD’s own account, it developed the seven-seat layout for the UK and Europe, a promotional video called the Ti7 the first seven-seat SUV “in Europe,” and BYD wouldn’t commit to keeping it out of the EU. That was enough for the court to find a threat of infringement.

So BYD’s EU entities can no longer import, produce, offer, sell, store or supply the Ti7. The order kicks in one week after the ruling is formally served, and it even covers BYD’s Hungarian unit, since the judge considered it conceivable the Ti7 could come out of the new Szeged factory.

The UK is a different story. The court said it has no jurisdiction over BYD UK and threw out JLR’s UK design claims, so British deliveries are still on for January 2027. That’s the one European market where BYD actually opened orders, pricing the Ti7 at £47,995, about £24,000 below the £71,840 plug-in Defender 110.

BYD said it “strongly disagrees” with the judgment and will appeal, adding that the Ti7 “is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights.” JLR told AFP it protects its intellectual property and takes legal action when necessary.

BYD has four weeks to appeal, but the injunction stays in force while it does. JLR, for its part, has six months to file a full case on the merits, or BYD can get the injunction lifted.

There’s more coming. JLR also has a separate case in Rotterdam over copyright and “slavish imitation,” with a hearing scheduled for Wednesday.

This whole thing started in August, when JLR had bailiffs raid BYD’s Dutch offices in Schiedam and Hoofddorp. The court later ordered JLR to destroy everything it seized, saying it didn’t need BYD’s internal files to make its design case. And it didn’t. JLR won on the design registration alone.

The Ti7 looks like a Defender. We said so when BYD first brought it to the UK, and so did pretty much everyone else. Chinese automakers have been building Defender lookalikes for years, but most of them stayed in China.

BYD brought one to the Defender’s home turf at a £24,000 discount, so a fight with JLR was always coming.

As a consumer, I would consider one element extremely different between the two vehicles -- build quality. Land Rover has a reputation in that department. So does BYD. I would buy the BYD on that alone in the BBB (big,boxy,brick) "category" of vehicle. Is that what JLR is really worried about?

But honestly, all these boxy SUVs look the same to me.

Nobody owns “boxy.” JLR even failed to trademark the classic Defender’s shape in the UK, a fight it lost in its legal battle with the Ineos Grenadier. But it registered the new Defender’s design in 2018, and that specific combination of shoulders, C-pillar panel and wheel arches is exactly what the court protected. That’s how design rights are supposed to work.

The actual business damage is small for now. The Ti7 sells roughly 30,000 units a month, almost all in China, and the UK launch goes ahead. The stock dip was about headlines more than lost Ti7 sales.

#4199. Honkai: Star Rail 3.8 will run for an extra two weeks while Version 4.0 is in the oven

The next Honkai: Star Rail update is upon us, and there's a mix of good - and unusual news.

HoYoverse just hosted a sizeable Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, revealing more than just the game’s next major update. Version 3.8 was the big highlight, of course, with the new release arriving soon, on December 16-17 depending on your server region.

Alongside showing everything coming with this next update, the developer also announced that 3.8 will go on for eight weeks, rather than the usual six. V3.8 is dubbed "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams", and it brings an end to the Amphoreus journey.

The story in "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams" takes place after the final battle of Amphoreus, where Constance "The Dahlia" appears to deliver a twist: the Trailblazer's memories are scattered, with many parts missing.

This final quest revolves around finding them in order to piece together the mystery, and involves a return to Penacony. This memory-hunting adventure is told from the perspective of Firefly, which will also explain how she entered the dreamscape initially and met the squad.

The new playable character is The Dahlia, whose power is linked to the the Remembrance path, which allows her to fabricate memories. Despite taking her powers from the Remembrance, The Dhalia actually follows the Path of Nihility in-game: she’s a 5-Star character who shines in teams dealing Break DMG.

The Dhalia can unleash a Gloomy Zone that causes Toughness Reduction inflicted by allies to trigger Super Break DMG, even before you break your enemies’ Weaknesses. The Dahlia can also invite one teammate to become her Dance Partner, which allows them (and her) to deal additional Super Break DMG each time they attack an enemy. If you trigger her Ultimate after picking a Dance Partner, she applies Type Weaknesses of both partners to enemies.

While The Dahlia is the only new character appearing in this final Amphoreus update, there'll be reruns aplenty, with an unusual third banner phase to make up for the extra long wait for 4.0. Appropriately for her role in the story, Firefly will make her return alongside The Dahlia in Phase 1, while Fugue and Lingsha will both have banner reruns in Phase 2, which is expected on January 7th. A bonus two-week-long Phase 3 will then begin on January 28th, seeing brief reappearances for popular returning characters Aglaea and Sunday, before things (presumably) go back to normal with the new annual update.

Something else to look forward to in 3.8 is The Chrysos Awoo Championship, which invites players to become chimera trainers and compete in team-based battles. The Remnants of Twilight event kicks off with the new patch, too, featuring its own set of challenges. However, HoYoverse have confirmed that there won't be an extra event during Phase 3 — but hopefully that'll give you some time to wrap up the last of the Amphoreus story content, which is longer than the previous four chapters put together.

#4197. For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard

How often you exercise may matter more for your mental health than how hard you push yourself during a workout. A large study of Norwegian college students found that those who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety one year later. The findings suggest that maintaining a consistent exercise routine could be particularly important for supporting mental well-being.

The research, published in the open access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Michael Grasdalsmoen of Western Norway University of Applied Sciences and his colleagues. Their results point to the potential benefits of exercising regularly rather than focusing primarily on longer or more demanding workouts.

Why Exercise Habits Matter for Mental Health

Depression, anxiety, and other common mental health conditions are among the leading causes of disability in young adults worldwide. The college years can be an especially challenging period as students adjust to new academic, social, and personal responsibilities. Identifying everyday behaviors that may help protect mental health is therefore an important research priority.

Although previous research has linked regular physical activity to better psychological well-being, many young adults remain physically inactive. Scientists have also had relatively limited evidence about how exercise habits relate to the development of mental health conditions over time, particularly when those conditions are evaluated using standardized diagnostic tools.

To investigate this relationship, Grasdalsmoen and his team followed 10,460 full-time students enrolled in higher education in Norway. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 35.

At the beginning of the study, students completed questionnaires describing their exercise habits, including how frequently they worked out, how strenuous their activities were, how long they exercised, and how many total hours they were active each week. One year later, they completed a self-administered diagnostic assessment designed to identify common mental health disorders.

Exercise Frequency May Matter More Than Intensity

The researchers found that students who reported lower levels of physical activity were more likely to meet diagnostic criteria for anxiety or depression one year later. However, not every aspect of exercise showed the same relationship with mental health.

Exercise frequency emerged as a particularly consistent factor. How often students exercised was more reliably associated with their later mental health than the intensity of their workouts or the amount of time they spent exercising.

The researchers also identified differences between men and women. Among women, lower exercise intensity was associated with a greater likelihood of anxiety and depression. Among men, spending fewer total hours exercising each week showed a stronger association with these conditions.

Overall, the likelihood of common mental health disorders decreased as weekly exercise increased, with this pattern continuing up to approximately 10 hours of physical activity per week.

The results also support the World Health Organization's recommendation that adults complete at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity each week.

Regular Exercise Could Help Support Student Mental Health

Taken together, the findings suggest that exercising consistently may be especially valuable for reducing the likelihood of anxiety and depression among college students. Rather than concentrating exclusively on workout intensity or duration, maintaining a regular routine could be an important part of supporting mental health.

However, the researchers emphasize that their observational study cannot establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship. Although students who exercised more regularly tended to have better mental health outcomes, the results do not prove that exercise itself prevented depression or anxiety.

Even with this limitation, promoting accessible opportunities for physical activity could be a useful part of broader efforts to improve student well-being. Such efforts may be especially relevant for students who are beginning to experience mental health difficulties or symptoms that have not yet reached the threshold for a clinical diagnosis.

The authors add: "Our findings show that students who engage in regular physical exercise are at lower risk of developing common mental disorders over time. These findings highlight the importance of making physical activity an accessible and natural part of student life."

"Mental health among students is a growing public health concern. Our findings suggest that supporting students to be physically active may contribute to better mental health and should be recognized as an important part of a healthy learning environment."

Subaru vehicles are known for their dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) capabilities, but to cut costs, the company is now offering front-wheel-drive (FWD) versions on select electric models.

The Uncharted EV went on sale earlier this year as a smaller, sportier entry-level electric crossover positioned below the Solterra.

It was also the first Subaru model in about 30 years not to come with standard all-wheel drive. After unveiling the Uncharted EV last summer, Subaru said, “For buyers focused on affordability and range, the entry-level Uncharted Premium FWD model will be offered in limited numbers.”

Apparently, it wasn’t too limited. The 2027 Uncharted EV is now on sale, still with the base Premium FWD model equipped with a single 221-horsepower front-mounted electric motor.

Higher-priced Uncharted trims, including the Sport and GT, are upgraded with Subaru’s Symmetrical All-Wheel Drive system with X-Mode, delivering a combined 338 horsepower.

The 2027 Subaru Uncharted EV Premium FWD starts at $34,995, while the Sport and GT are priced from $39,795 and $43,795, respectively.

In the US, the 2027 Solterra and larger Trailseeker are still equipped with standard AWD, but Subaru is introducing new FWD (4×2) variants in some markets at a lower price point.

In comparison, the 2027 Subaru Solterra and Trailseeker EV start at $38,495 and $39,995, respectively.

Subaru opened preorders for its new 2027 electric range in Spain, including the Unchartered, Solterra, and E-Outback, which is sold as the Trailseeker in the US.

All of which will be available with a lower-priced FWD variant. Like the Uncharted, Subaru will still offer AWD on higher-priced Solterra and E-Outback trims.

Will Subaru expand FWD (4×2) to other vehicles and markets, like the US? The Uncharted is still Subaru’s only EV sold with standard FWD. The 2027 Solterra and Trailseeker are equipped with AWD and X-Mode.

#4194. Tomorrow’s Battlefield 6 patch is the first step towards improving footstep audio, and it might actually fix the settings reset bug

The next major Battlefield 6 patch is nearly upon us, and Battlefield Studios is promising a bounty of changes - including a couple of fixes to some big bugs.

Battlefield 6 is about to receive a new update. Version 1.1.3.0 is set to arrive tomorrow, December 9 to kick off the third and final phase of the game’s first season. Winter Offensive brings some holiday-themed new content to the game, but it’s not the most interesting part of the patch.

That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the new patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.

Thew new content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly. To go along with that there are new limited-time modes for both multiplayer and Redsec’s Gauntlet. The event mode will be available in Conquest, and Domination.

The Ice Climbing Axe is the only new weapon in this drop. The battle pass gets a new Winter Offensive bonus path, just like we’ve seen with previous seasonal stages. This is how you unlock the axe, too.

Easily the most interesting change in this update is the range of improvements to audio across the board. First, footstep audio received a big pass that should make it easier to hear enemy footsteps, easier to locate them, and across different surfaces.

Some of the bugs that caused certain sounds to simply vanish have been fixed. This was especially prevalent in battle royale matches. BF Studios explained in the patch notes that it has adjusted memory priorities for in-game sounds in order to prioritise the most crucial ones. This is not the end of the road on audio, however, as the developer continues to work on making the soundscape more stable and reliable.

Some of those audio changes are the result of recent testing done in Battlefield Labs, which is also responsible for another exciting addition in this latest patch: improvements to hit registration.

While BF6 has had solid and stable netcode, certain situations would sometimes create uncertainty about how you died, and why certain actions seemingly failed to perform at that particular moment.

The focus in this update is to improve the reliability of how actions in close-quarter combat are translated, which includes firing before fully going into ADS, quick aim changes and more.

Speaking of close-range, the patch also brings another pass to soldier visibility to make it easier for enemies to stand out from the background. This is particularly relevant in areas with low contrast, or busy environments with lots of particle and visual effects.

1.1.3.0 also brings yet another set of weapon handling and gunplay tweaks, this time focusing on accuracy issues with first shots. You can also expect more tweaks to attachment behaviour with regards to recoil.

Something else worth highlighting is that vehicle gameplay is getting several smaller tweaks that have to do with how they interact with the world, how their HUDs behave and more. Finally, your settings should no longer be reset after applying an update. BF Studios says there are still some instances where that might happen, but the issue should be fixed for the majority of players.

You can read the full change log on the Battlefield blog.

#4193. Driven: 2027 Audi Q7 and SQ7 SUVs Muscle Up

Over the past two decades, if you were looking for an upscale three-row German SUV, the Audi Q7 or its performance-oriented SQ7 sibling was likely on your shopping list. Both have long delivered on style, family-friendliness, and luxury.

The mid-size Audi SUVs are completely new for 2027, but the automaker has been careful not to stray too far from a blueprint that has proved so successful. With this latest generation, the Q7’s design has been brought up to speed with the rest of the Audi lineup. That means softer edges, a more muscular stance, and a lot more digital displays inside.

While the Q7’s dimensions grow slightly in most directions, it’s still roughly the same size as before, and its three-row layout could best be described as a 5+2, as the cramped rearmost chairs are best used by children and only in a pinch. If you need more space, there’s now a full-size Q9 model that’s larger inside and out.

See all results for new 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near h2k 3g7

The Q7 does gain a sought-after second-row feature: optional captain’s chairs. Choosing the two-seat second row reduces seat count from seven to six, but it also decreases the risk of sibling quarrels.

Speaking of the cabin, we’ve complained that Audi’s latest interiors haven’t lived up to the standard set by the company’s earlier efforts, but the new Q7 represents a reversal of that trend. Granted, the models we sampled were well-optioned examples, but the interior materials are premium, and even the $72,295 base model gets genuine leather upholstery and real wood inlays.

Upgrade to a higher Q7 trim, and you’ll enjoy luxuries such as soft-close doors, a Bang & Olufsen stereo, and massaging front seats. The SQ7 comes in just one trim level, starting at $100,095, and it’s comprehensively equipped with only a few available packages, most of them designed to improve performance and handling.

Special attention has been paid to the SUV’s exterior lighting elements. There are a lot of them, and some are genuinely useful, none more so than Audi’s digital matrix headlights.

Not only do these high-tech headlamps deliver a shockingly bright view of the road ahead, but they also sense oncoming vehicles and will temporarily deactivate some of their bulbs to avoid blinding other motorists. A set of OLED taillights illuminate in different ways depending on context, with the intent to help communicate with other drivers: For example, if another vehicle is too close to the Q7’s rear bumper in traffic, the lights will illuminate with additional brightness as a warning to back off.

Other flashy features push into gimmick territory. There’s a light-up grille, a customizable taillamp and daytime-running-light signature, and a system that projects arrows on the street surface to indicate which direction the driver is signaling. Are blinkers no longer enough? Luckily, if you don’t want your Audi lighting up like a Christmas tree, some of these features can be deactivated via the Q7’s infotainment system.

See all results for new 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near h2k 3g7

Speaking of infotainment, there are a lot of screens inside the Q7. A large infotainment touchscreen is expected, surely, but there’s also a digital gauge display, a passenger’s display, and an optional head-up display.

While the previous-generation Q7 offered a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four as standard with a turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6 as an upgrade, the 2027 model ditches the four-banger altogether, making a V-6 standard. This version’s six—a turbo 2.9-liter—packs 429 horsepower, a 94-hp advantage over the outgoing model.

A twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8 has always powered the SQ7, and the new generation is no different. It also gets more power, jumping from 500 horsepower in 2026 to 591 horsepower in 2027.

Acceleration is plentiful in the Q7, which makes quick work of highway passing maneuvers and will beat most regular traffic off the line with a quick stab of the throttle. Audi estimates a 4.8-second 60-mph time.

The SQ7 is another animal altogether. While both SUVs have launch control, using it in the SQ7 results in a giggle-inducing run to highway speeds. Audi wagers a 60-mph run would take just 3.7 seconds. The V-8’s muted burble is a bonus.

Confident and predictable handling, an Audi touchstone, remains the default. While all Q7s come with Balanced, Dynamic, and Comfort drive modes, those with the optional air-spring suspension benefit most, with each mode delivering noticeably different ride qualities. SQ7s get air springs as standard but can be optioned with a sport-tuned version of the system, which lowers the ride height 1.2 inches in Dynamic mode and firms everything up to the max.

SQ7 models also feature a retuned all-wheel-drive system with more rear bias. Unlike previous Audi performance SUVs, which were short on driving drama, the new SQ7’s more fun-loving nature shines on twisty roads with that newfound rear-end boogie. Our test drive took us down some of northern California’s twistiest roads, and both SUVs proved entertaining and luxurious.

With this new generation, Audi has boosted the Q7 and SQ7’s swank factor. It has modernized their styling without introducing a new polarizing design language while adding options buyers want. Retaining the Q7’s just-right size and keeping the focus on refined, performance-oriented road manners is the hedge that will keep it near the top of the shopping list of enthusiast drivers who need family-sized space.

#4190. Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months

A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a new clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating. Researchers found that people following a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet experienced substantially greater reductions in liver fat than those eating Mediterranean or low-fat diets, even though all three groups lost similar amounts of weight.

The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes. After just four to five months on a ketogenic (or "Keto") diet, approximately half of the participants no longer met the diagnostic criteria for the condition. The findings, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, suggest that the types of foods people eat can influence metabolic health in ways that extend beyond the number of pounds they lose.

"We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," says Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. "Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have important therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone."

Comparing Keto, Mediterranean, and Low-Fat Diets

An estimated 40% of American adults have obesity, a condition associated with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and other health problems. Doctors frequently recommend dietary changes to help patients lose weight and improve their metabolic health, which refers to how effectively the body manages energy, blood sugar, and fats.

Three commonly recommended approaches are low-carbohydrate diets, low-fat diets, and Mediterranean diets. Although each can support weight loss, researchers have been uncertain whether one offers additional metabolic advantages when the amount of weight lost is roughly the same.

These eating patterns differ substantially in their nutritional makeup. Low-carbohydrate approaches, including Atkins and ketogenic diets, restrict carbohydrate consumption, while low-fat diets may obtain as much as 70% of their calories from carbohydrates. The Mediterranean diet emphasizes plant foods such as vegetables, nuts, and olive oil, along with moderate amounts of fish and dairy. Ketogenic diets, meanwhile, can include considerable amounts of fat from animal products, including saturated fat.

To compare their effects, Klein and his colleagues recruited 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Prediabetes occurs when blood sugar levels rise above the normal range but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver disease involves excess fat accumulating inside liver cells, which can interfere with the body's ability to regulate metabolism.

A Controlled Clinical Trial With Similar Weight Loss

Participants were randomly assigned to follow one of three diets: ketogenic, Mediterranean, or a low-fat diet emphasizing plant-based foods. To ensure that participants followed their assigned eating plans, the research team supplied all their meals and arranged weekly consultations with a dietitian.

The diets had sharply different proportions of carbohydrates and fat. In the ketogenic group, carbohydrates accounted for just 4% of daily calories, while fat supplied 73%. The Mediterranean group received 50% of its calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat. The plant-forward group consumed 70% of its calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.

Researchers adjusted calorie intake individually so that participants across all three groups lost approximately 10% of their starting body weight. Reaching this target took about four to five months.

By the end of the intervention, every group had experienced meaningful reductions in body fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. Greater insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

However, the similarities between the groups largely ended there.

The ketogenic diet produced the largest improvements in several important indicators of liver function and metabolic health.

Participants following keto experienced an average 67% reduction in liver fat, compared with a 45% reduction in both the Mediterranean and low-fat groups. Because the groups lost comparable amounts of weight, the difference suggests that carbohydrate restriction may influence liver fat through mechanisms beyond weight loss alone.

To investigate these effects, the researchers collected blood samples repeatedly over a 24-hour period, allowing them to observe changes in hormones involved in energy metabolism.

The ketogenic group showed the greatest increase in glucagon, a hormone that helps regulate the body's energy supply and promotes the reduction of fat stored in the liver. Participants on keto also experienced the largest decrease in insulin levels, another change that can help reduce liver fat accumulation.

One result was particularly unexpected. Despite getting nearly three-quarters of their calories from fat, the keto participants did not show an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels during the study.

"The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn't experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels despite consuming the most fat," says Max Petersen, the study's first author at Washington University School of Medicine.

Half of Keto Participants No Longer Had Prediabetes

The benefits extended beyond liver fat. After the weight-loss intervention, approximately 50% of participants assigned to the ketogenic diet no longer met the criteria for prediabetes. By comparison, that milestone was reached by 29% of those on the Mediterranean diet and just 7% of those following the low-fat, plant-forward diet.

These differences are notable because prediabetes signals an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Bringing blood sugar levels below the prediabetes threshold is an important improvement, although it does not necessarily mean the condition has been permanently reversed.

The findings also highlight a potentially important distinction in weight management: losing weight and improving metabolic health are closely connected, but they are not necessarily the same thing. The composition of a diet may affect how the body handles blood sugar, stores fat, and responds to hormones, even when weight loss is similar.

Researchers emphasize the growing importance of understanding these effects as powerful new obesity treatments become more widely available. GLP-1 medications, which act on hormone pathways involved in appetite and blood sugar regulation, have transformed the treatment of obesity by helping many patients achieve substantial weight loss.

"GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss," Petersen says. "But in addition, our study shows that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits."

Although the trial was relatively small and lasted only four to five months, its carefully controlled design offers evidence that dietary composition can play an important role in metabolic health. Longer studies involving more participants will be needed to determine whether the benefits persist and how different diets compare over time.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

#4188. One of the world’s biggest zinc mines is getting Alaska’s largest solar farm

Red Dog Mine in Alaska burns about 40,000 gallons of diesel a day to keep one of the world’s largest zinc mines running, and now, an 8.8-megawatt (MW) solar farm and battery storage will help cut that fuel use.

The Alaska Energy Authority’s board unanimously approved a nearly $5 million loan for the project through its Power Project Fund. Tugliq Red Dog1 will build, own, and operate the roughly $35 million solar project and sell the electricity to mine operator Teck Alaska. The state’s loan review says site work began in June and expects the solar and storage to come online in October 2028.

Red Dog sits about 105 miles north of the Arctic Circle, on land owned by NANA, an Iñupiat-owned Alaska Native corporation. The array would be larger than any solar farm operating in Alaska today, as KOTZ’s Desiree Hagen reported for Alaska Public Media. Hagen reported that the plans call for more than 15,000 panels across around 30 acres.

The mine gets all its power from on-site diesel generators. In summer, it can draw so much electricity that Teck has to cut power elsewhere at the site. The solar array and the 8.8 MW, 15 megawatt-hour (MWh) battery will give the operator another source of power during those crunches.

The state of Alaska expects the solar and storage project to cover about 5% of the zinc mine’s electricity needs under its current operating plan. The project could do even more after mining ends, covering about 90% of the site’s annual electricity needs.

Teck expects the mine’s existing deposits to support operations through 2031, and it’s studying whether to develop two nearby deposits. If that expansion goes ahead, the state projects the solar and battery project would cover about 3% of the larger operation’s electricity needs. If mining ends, demand will drop sharply, but the site will still need electricity for cleanup and long-term water treatment.

#4187. Battlefield 6's latest update dubbed the game's simultaneously best and worst patch as it runs into all kinds of issues

What's likely going to be the last major Battlefield 6 update of the year has launched with a number of unexpected issues.

There’s been a lot of anticipation for Battlefield 6’s version 1.1.3.0 patch. The patch kicks off the third and final phase of the game’s first season, adding some new holiday-themed content. More the new content itself, the update’s biggest additions are almost entirely gameplay-related.

Unfortunately, for as much as the changes in 1.1.3.0 have been well received, the launch has been marred by a series of technical issues, some of which are a little unusual.

Immediately after patch 1.1.3.0 went live, players on PC started reporting massive stutters that would occur every few seconds. The issue is especially pronounced in Redsec Battle Royale, but much deadlier in traditional multiplayer.

Battlefield Studios quickly acknowledged it, pointing out a workaround that appears to be working for players on Steam. According to those players, going offline on Steam’s friends menu has fixed stuttering for them.

The issue remains for other players on PC, however, and the developer said it’s working on a proper fix.

Perhaps the most disrupting problem the patch has caused is one that prevents players from being able to interact with the game’s menu. Tiles become unresponsive, or outright unselectable when you try to hover near them.

Ironically, the top set of tiles designed to make it easy for players to quickly jump into the new content has been the most affected. Restarting the game sometimes fixes the issue, and some players report that it only happens upon first launch after installing the update.

But Battlefield Studios later clarified that, unsurprisingly, there’s an actual reason behind the bug. Once again, a fix is being investigated, and the developer will offer an update once some progress has been made.

A little further down the list of importance is an issue that stops players from being able to skip tiers within the new Winter Offensive bonus path in the game’s battle pass. BF Studios took out the feature entirely while it works on a fix, so while you can continue making progress in the bonus path, you won’t be able to skip tiers.

This is all a shame to see. Outside of all the problems, the meat of the new update has been almost universally praised. The visibility improvements, and netcode updates have been celebrated. Many players were also happy to see meaningful updates to footstep audio and overall clarity.

It’s also unusual for a Battlefield 6 patch to run into so many issues at launch. The sentiment around 1.1.3.0 so far is that it’s the game’s best and worst update yet. Hopefully those issues will be fixed before the development team breaks for the holidays.

#4185. Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

Plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings. However, new research suggests that this assumption may not hold when plastic breaks down into extremely small particles.

As larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically. Scientists have now discovered that these newly exposed surfaces can interact with water in unexpected ways, producing reactive molecules that may harm living cells.

Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a new study published in Nature. Their findings challenge the longstanding idea that microplastics are simply passive fragments of material.

"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously. Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals (reactive oxygen species, ROS) that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure," said Wei Min, a Columbia professor of Chemistry and Biomedical Engineering.

Why Microplastics Could Be Dangerous Inside the Human Body

The discovery raises important questions about what happens when microplastics enter the human body. Blood and cells contain large amounts of water, creating conditions in which these tiny particles could continue participating in chemical reactions.

Rather than remaining inactive after exposure, microplastics may generate reactive oxygen species, often called ROS. These highly reactive molecules can damage biological structures, including components of cells and tissues. The findings offer a possible explanation for some of the harmful effects associated with microplastic exposure, although they do not establish that this process causes specific diseases in humans.

The research builds on earlier work by Min's laboratory that helped reveal just how widespread microscopic plastic contamination has become.

In a widely reported 2024 study, the Columbia researchers developed a laser-based microscopy technique capable of detecting extremely small plastic particles. Using this technology, they found an average of approximately 240,000 detectable plastic fragments in a single liter of bottled water (mostly nanometer-sized plastic, nanoplastics). That was 10 to 100 times more particles than previous estimates had suggested.

The discovery helped draw greater attention to the presence of microplastics and nanoplastics throughout the food system.

Growing Concerns About Microplastics and Human Health

Since that earlier research attracted widespread attention, the potential health consequences of microplastic exposure have become an increasingly important public health issue.

In 2026, the federal government launched a $144 million initiative focused on addressing toxic microplastics in the human body. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also added microplastics to a federal list of contaminants that may be of concern in drinking water, marking their first appearance on the list.

Meanwhile, studies published in major scientific journals, including the New England Journal of Medicine, Nature Medicine, and Nature Health, have reported associations between exposure to microplastics and nanoplastics and serious conditions such as heart attacks, strokes, dementia, and brain tumors.

However, an important question has remained unanswered. If plastic is generally considered chemically inert, how might these microscopic fragments contribute to biological damage?

The new findings identify a previously overlooked chemical pathway that could help researchers understand these potential health risks.

"Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate what we call reactive oxygen species (ROS)," said Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Wei Min's lab who helped lead the research. "ROS are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue."

How Water Triggers Harmful Chemical Reactions

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is that water plays an active role in the reaction.

Many plastics are hydrophobic, meaning their surfaces repel water. When water encounters these surfaces, the molecules and electrically charged particles near the boundary can behave differently than they do in ordinary water.

The researchers found that these interactions can encourage electrons to move between chemical species, allowing highly reactive radicals to form. As plastic fragments become smaller, their greater surface area provides more locations where these reactions can occur.

"Water is a key active player here, rather than just a spectator. It's integral to making these microplastics reactive. Water molecules become chemically active when they come into contact with plastic, which is hydrophobic. Contact between the water and plastic creates an environment that facilitates electron transfer, and the formation of reactive radicals. When plastics fragment into smaller particles, their increasing surface-to-volume ratio creates more of these chemically active areas," Min said.

To investigate the process, the Columbia researchers performed chemical and biological experiments. Their collaborators in Professor Teresa Head-Gordon's laboratory at UC Berkeley used theoretical calculations and computer simulations to examine the interactions between plastic surfaces and water at the molecular level.

The Berkeley team developed a theoretical explanation showing how hydroxide ions, which are negatively charged particles, can become concentrated in the layers of water immediately surrounding a water-repelling plastic surface. In this environment, the ions can more readily lose electrons and form hydroxyl radicals.

Hydroxyl radicals are particularly reactive chemical species capable of damaging biological molecules. Their formation provides a possible link between the physical breakdown of plastics and the biological effects researchers have observed.

Could the Discovery Lead to Safer Plastics?

Understanding the chemistry involved could eventually help scientists develop plastics that are less likely to generate harmful reactive molecules when exposed to water.

"Our fundamental work that the most hydrophobic microplastics interacting with water can drive chemical reactivity could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment," said Head-Gordon.

The implications also extend beyond human health. Microplastics can enter rivers, lakes, and other waterways through industrial waste, wastewater, and everyday activities. The newly identified chemical reactions could influence aquatic organisms and ecosystems exposed to these particles.

Co-author Beizhan Yan of Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory emphasized that microplastics can originate from numerous sources, including plastic manufacturing facilities and laundromats. Everyday processes, such as heating materials in a microwave or leaving bottled water exposed to sunlight during storage, can also contribute to the formation of tiny plastic particles.

"This work has significant implications for environmental and human health," said co-author Beizhan Yan of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "In certain environments, such as discharges from plastic manufacturers and laundromats, microplastics can form and enter aquatic environments. This work also indicates that radicals can form on hydrophobic plastic surfaces in water, which could affect ecosystems and human health following exposure. In addition, various uses and processes in our daily lives can generate microplastics, including microwave heating, sunlight exposure of bottled water during storage. This foundational work provides a potential pathway for understanding their health impacts."

By revealing that microplastics can actively alter the chemistry of surrounding water, the research adds a new dimension to concerns about plastic pollution. It also establishes a potential mechanism for investigating how these widespread particles interact with living systems, while opening the door to strategies for reducing their environmental and health risks.

#4184. Arc Raiders gets a few map exploit fixes in latest patch as Embark prepares to slow down how often patches are released

There's a new Arc Raiders patch that's fairly small, but one with fixes everyone is going to appreciate.

The time has arrived for another Arc Raiders update, and Embark has certainly delivered. Today’s patch, version 1.6.0, is among the smallest the game has received so far, focusing almost exclusively on disabling map exploits.

Perhaps more important than the patch itself, however, is the announcement the developer made around it.

Starting off with patch 1.6.0, it takes out a particular zipline on Stella Montis, the game’s most recent addition ot the map roster. Some players used said zipline to get out of bounds, something the game has been battling on several of its maps.

On Blue Gate, the patch fixes a collision issue that allowed players to vault through a wall, and fall to their death. The map fixes continue with another on Spaceport Launch Tower, which takes out a gap in collision that players have been able to shoot through.

The last change in this update affects gameplay feel around Arc enemies. Certain materials in the game’s world weren’t blocking their vision - or fire - when they should have, and this has now been fixed.

Alongside today’s patch, Embark also announced that going forward, we’re going to see fewer patches for Arc Raiders. The game has been getting updates almost every Thursday since it launched in late October.

Now that most of the major problems have been fixed, the studio is shifting to a slower patching cadence. Critical fixes will still be issued as soon as they’re developed, but don’t expect a patch each week going forward.

Embark also revealed that patch releases and in-game store rotations will now occur on Tuesdays. You should also expect the next few weeks to be quiet, as members of the team go on holiday breaks.

But, before everyone goes away, the game is going to get one more big update. The last item on Arc Raiders’ roadmap, revealed in early November, is the Cold Snap event. This is on track for Tuesday, bringing some new content alongside a few other fixes.

#4181. NASA's powerful Moon rocket engine roars through a dramatic 200-second test

NASA has successfully completed another powerful rocket engine test as the agency prepares for future Artemis missions that will return astronauts to the Moon and lay the groundwork for human exploration of Mars.

On November 18, engineers fired RS-25 engine No. 10001 at the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA's Stennis Space Center, located near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. The developmental engine ran for its full scheduled duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds).

Although this particular engine is not intended for spaceflight, the successful test will provide NASA and its primary contractor, L3Harris Technologies, with valuable performance data. Engineers will use the results to improve the power, efficiency, and reliability of RS-25 engines designed for upcoming Artemis missions.

Powerful RS-25 Engines Will Help Send Astronauts Back to the Moon

NASA is preparing for Artemis IV, a mission scheduled for 2028 that aims to land astronauts on the lunar surface. The mission will launch from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, using the massive Space Launch System (SLS) rocket to carry astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft.

Artemis IV represents an important step toward NASA's larger ambitions. The agency plans to explore the Moon's South Pole, establish a sustained human presence on the lunar surface, and develop the experience and technologies needed for the first crewed journey to Mars.

The RS-25 engines play a crucial role in making these missions possible. Each SLS rocket uses four of the engines, which together generate up to 2 million pounds of thrust to help propel the spacecraft off the launchpad and into space.

Before any RS-25 engine is cleared for flight, it must undergo testing at NASA's Stennis Space Center to verify that it can perform reliably under the extreme conditions of a rocket launch.

These tests are carried out by specialists from NASA, L3Harris Technologies, and Nova Space Solutions, working together to ensure the engines are ready to power future journeys beyond Earth.

#4180. Driven: 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA EV Is Both Familiar and a First

The electric Benz hatchback shares much with its CLA EV sibling.

At the debut of the redesigned Mercedes-Benz GLA, company chairman Ola Källenius said, “The ICE [internal-combustion engine] world and the BEV [battery-electric vehicle] world have come together.” And that’s true: Apart from their grilles, the gas-engine GLA and the first-ever GLA EV are virtually indistinguishable from each other. Källenius described the design of the new GLA as “clearly electric-first,” so it’s perhaps appropriate that the EV version is the first one we’re driving.

Electric-first is also the go-to-market strategy—at least in Europe. It was to be in the U.S., too, but there’s been a reversal; we’re now slated to get the GLA hybrid first. Really, though, we won’t be getting either one for a while. We’re told to expect the gas-engine GLA sometime late next year, while the EV won’t arrive until the first half of 2028. Our recent drive of the electric GLA in Spain, therefore, was an extra-long-lead preview.

See all results for new 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA-Class EV for sale near l7a 0b5

We’d say that gives buyers plenty of time to warm up to the new styling, except that the look is not all that different from the current GLA. More substantial, maybe: The body is bigger, sitting astride a wheelbase that is stretched 2.4 inches. The new GLA is also longer, lower, and wider.

The GLA EV is also adorned with more three-pointed stars, though not to the extent of some other recent Mercedes products. Besides the illuminated logo on the flat-panel “grille,” there’s a large badge on the rear liftgate, and the motif also appears in the headlights and taillights. Opt for Sky Control for the standard glass roof panel, and 172 light-up stars appear on the glass, which is electronically dimmable in sections.

The dash is lifted straight from the GLA’s sedan sibling, the CLA. As in other Benz models, there’s an available Superscreen that adds a 14.0-inch passenger display to the standard 14.0-inch center touchscreen and 10.3-inch instrument screen. With it, virtually the entire dashboard is given over to digital real estate. Sadly, almost none of the space contains any physical switchgear, although at least we still get air vents that can be aimed by hand. Wireless smartphone mirroring is standard, but a wireless charging pad costs extra. The navigation uses Google Maps and optionally offers Benz’s augmented reality, an inset showing a forward-camera view with overlaid arrows indicating direction. Unfortunately, that inset appears on the left side of the touchscreen, where it’s obscured by the driver’s right hand on the wheel; you have to peer around to see it.

The on-screen climate controls are another ergonomic fail, as the touch points to change the temperature are tiny, and you have to open the climate menu to adjust the fan speed. You could ask for help from Benz’s digital assistant, which lurks within the screen, always listening. And there’s a camera trained on the driver, which can use facial recognition to automatically call up the driver’s profile and saved preferences. It can also take selfies! Beyond the digital, the interior features high-back front seats that are firmly padded and well shaped. The high center console makes for a somewhat confining feel up front, but its floating design creates a large open bay underneath for storage. The rear-seat area boasts a flat floor and is much roomier than in the CLA sedan. The cargo hold is 15 cubic feet, expandable to 49 cubes with the rear seatbacks folded. There’s also a frunk that’s about the size of a carry-on suitcase.

The powertrains mirror the CLA EV’s. There’s a single-motor GLA250+ that sends 268 horsepower to the rear wheels. The dual-motor GLA350 4Matic has all-wheel drive and 349 horses. Both employ a two-speed transmission on the rear axle for improved efficiency at highway speeds.

The standard suspension has passive dampers, but the cars we drove had the optional adaptive dampers and rode on 20-inch wheels (18s are standard; 19s are also available). The smooth pavement of Barcelona and sunny coastal environs gave the dampers little to adapt to—any real assessment of the GLA’s ride quality will have to wait until we drive one on the meaner streets back home. However, the suspension acquitted itself well on our drive route’s long series of hillside curves. The GLA is composed but would be more confidence-inspiring if the steering weren’t so light and remote.

The GLA isn’t a hot hatch, though; it’s more of an urban runabout. In that context, the 268-hp GLA250+ is adequately peppy, even though Mercedes posits a rather languid 60-mph time of 7.2 seconds. We expect it to do better than that, as the CLA250+ we tested managed a 5.8-second result. The dual-motor GLA350 felt much more energetic, particularly outside of urban environs, where it quickly passed dawdlers on two-lane roads and merged easily onto the freeway. For the GLA350, Mercedes claims a 5.3-second 60-mph time, but again that’s likely an undersell; testing a mechanically identical CLA350, we got 4.3 seconds. Even so, there are quicker EVs in this class, but one positive here is that even the higher-horsepower dual-motor version doesn’t feel like its output overwhelms its chassis—often an issue with high-horsepower EVs. Besides the standard drive modes of Eco, Comfort, Sport, and Individual, the dual-motor GLA adds a Terrain mode that optimizes the powertrain for loose surfaces; its camera system is able to stitch together a “transparent hood” view of what’s immediately in front of the car.

When it comes time for slowing, there are three levels of liftoff regen (D, D+, and D-), as well as an Auto setting that varies the regen level based on info from the navigation system and the forward-facing cameras. Our preference is D-, which is essentially coasting, but D+ will please fans of one-pedal driving. We also tried the automated parking function, which was able to back into and out of a parallel-parking spot without trying our patience. It’s a digital add-on that’s purchased for a set time period; the same goes for the MBUX Entertainment package of multimedia streaming and app downloads.

Like the CLA EV sedan, the GLA is built on Benz’s MMA platform, with an 800-volt architecture and an 85-kWh battery. That architecture allows for speedy DC recharging, up to 320 kilowatts. Should you find a power source robust enough to reach that figure, Mercedes says the GLA battery can go from 10 percent to 80 percent in 22 minutes. (In our testing of the CLA250+ with the same hardware, it went from 10 to 80 percent in just 21 minutes.) EPA range estimates for the GLA aren’t yet available, but the CLA offers a clue, and its impressive range figures run from 312 miles on the low end to as high as 374 miles.

If the GLA ends up with numbers like those, it’ll look pretty good against the electric Mini Countryman, Genesis GV60, and Cadillac Optiq, and similar-ish to a Rivian R2. Those look to be the GLA EV’s prime competitors at a base-price guesstimate of around $50K. But the EV landscape could shift significantly by the time the GLA gets here. After all, a lot can happen between now and 2028.
